question.:question/problem:
Find the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=3 - x^{2}$ at the point $(2,-1).$

$x\,-$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=3 - x^{2}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(3 - x^{2}\right)=- 2 x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,-1):$

$$
m=f'(2)=-4
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-1)&=\frac{1}{4}(x-(2)) \\ x - 4 y&=6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
m={f}^{′}(\frac{1}{8})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt[3]{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{2}}}=2

question.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{5}-2x$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=ax+b$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants. Find the value of $a+b.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{5}-2x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{5}-2x)=10{x}^{4}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m &={f}^{′}(1)=10(1)^{4}-2=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-\frac{1}{8}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{8}+\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a+b=-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{8}=0.$

generation.domain: real x; positive x for radical/reciprocal; tangent slope nonzero

question.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}$ at the point $(1,4)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $q-p.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =-2{x}^{-3/2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m &={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{1}^{3}}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ 2y-8 & =x-1 \\ x-2y & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q-p=-7-(-2)=-5.$

question.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x$ at the point $(1,3)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p-q.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-2}-x) \\  & =-8{x}^{-3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m &={f}^{′}(1)=-8(1)^{-3}-1=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(3) & =\frac{1}{9}(x-1) \\ 9y-27 & =x-1 \\ x-9y & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p-q=-9-(-26)=17.$

Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x-2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}-x-2) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-2}-x) \\  & =-8{x}^{-3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m &={f}^{′}(1)=-8(1)^{-3}-1=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$

question.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=3{x}^{2}+4x$ at the point $(1,7)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p+q.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=3{x}^{2}+4x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}+4x)=6x+4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,7):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m &={f}^{′}(1)=6(1)+4=10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(7) & =-\frac{1}{10}(x-1) \\ 10y-70 & =-x+1 \\ x+10y & =71.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p+q=10+71=81.$

question.:question/problem:
The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{3}$ at the point $(2,16)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $q-p.$

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{3}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3})=6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,16):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m &={f}^{'}(2)=6(2)^{2}=24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{'}$ is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{24}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(16) & =-\frac{1}{24}(x-(2)) \\ 24y-384 & =-x+2 \\ x+24y & =386.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q-p=386-24=362.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-2)=6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,14):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m &={f}^{'}(2)=6(2)^{2}=24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{'}$ is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{24}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(14) & =-\frac{1}{24}(x-(2)) \\ 24 y - 336 & =-x+2 \\ x+24y & =338.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y = 2x^{2}$ at the point $(2, 8)$ is given by $x + py = q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p + q$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2 x^{2}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(2 x^{2}\right)=4 x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,8):$

$$
m=f'(2)=8
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=- \frac{1}{8}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(8)&=- \frac{1}{8}(x-(2)) \\ x + 8 y&=66.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p+q=74.$

The equation of the normal to the curve $y=f(x)\cdot h(x)$ at the point where $x=\pi$ is

question.:question/worked-solution:
When $x=\pi ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\pi ) & =f(\pi )\cdot h(\pi ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{\pi }\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{\pi }\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

In part 3, we found that the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)\cdot h(x)$ at the point where $x=\pi$ is $m=2{e}^{\pi }.$ Therefore, the slope of the normal ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{2{e}^{\pi }}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =-\frac{1}{2{e}^{\pi }}(x-\pi ) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2{e}^{\pi }}+\frac{\pi }{2{e}^{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$
